findings.situation: A self-employed filer or partner received benefits under a dependent care assistance program from their own sole proprietorship or partnership, for example reported on Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) box 13 code O, and has no W-2 box 10 amount or grace-period carryover, so they answer no.
findings.source_text: f2441 (2025) p. 2, line 12: "If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership"; i2441 (2025) p. 1: "Benefits you received as a partner should be shown in box 13 of your Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) with code O."
findings.why: The question defines dependent care benefits as only W-2 box 10 amounts or a 2024 grace-period carryover. A filer whose benefits came from their own business answers no, so Part III and the line 1e taxable amount are skipped even though the benefits must be counted on line 12.

findings.situation: An employee received dependent care benefits that the employer did not show in W-2 box 10, such as on-site daycare or direct payments to a provider that were left out, and answers no because nothing appears in box 10.
findings.source_text: i2441 (2025) p. 1, Definitions: "Dependent care benefits may include: • Amounts your employer paid directly to either you or your care provider ... • The fair market value of care in a daycare facility provided or sponsored by your employer ... If you received dependent care benefits as an employee, they should be shown in box 10"
findings.why: The text treats box 10 as where benefits should be reported, not as what defines them. The question's "amounts shown in box 10" wording leads a filer with unreported benefits to answer no, although Form 2441 Part III is still required.

findings.situation: A filer paid for care of a disabled parent who lived with them more than half of 2025 but whom they cannot claim as a dependent only because the parent had gross income of $5,200 or more. The filer reads 'a dependent or spouse who was not able to care for themselves' and truthfully answers no.
findings.source_text: i2441 p. 1, Qualifying Person(s): "Any disabled person ... whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except: a. The disabled person had gross income of $5,200 or more, b. The disabled person filed a joint return, or c. You (or your spouse if filing jointly) could be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2025 tax return."
findings.why: The question limits qualifying persons other than a spouse to 'a dependent', so it leaves out the 'could claim as a dependent except' group. Those filers answer no. That blocks f2441.filing and s3 line 2, and also f2441.nondependent_gate, which exists to handle exactly these persons.

findings.situation: A filer paid their 17-year-old child, or their spouse, to watch a younger child so the filer could work, and truthfully answers yes.
findings.source_text: Question: "did you ... pay for, or incur expenses for, the care of a qualifying person"; i2441 p. 3: "No credit is allowed for any amount paid to your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child ... provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by the end of the year and they can't be your dependent."
findings.why: The question does not exclude payments to ineligible related providers. A filer whose only care payments went to such a provider still answers yes. That switches on Form 2441 filing and the s3 line 2 credit path, even though these expenses cannot support the credit.

findings.situation: An employer provides on-site or employer-contracted child care, but the filer is not covered by an employer dependent care plan (for example, the care is a perk outside any dependent care assistance program); the filer truthfully answers yes.
findings.source_text: i2441 p. 3, Columns (a) and (b): "If you were covered by your employer's dependent care plan and your employer furnished the care (either at your workplace or by hiring a care provider), enter your employer's name in column (a)"
findings.why: The question asks only whether the employer furnished the care. It drops the instructions' first condition, coverage under the employer's dependent care plan, so filers outside a plan answer yes and trigger the employer-furnished treatment.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse's employer plan let the spouse carry forward unused 2024 benefits that the spouse used during the 2025 grace period, but the filer answers zero because the question asks only about 'your employer's dependent care plan'.
findings.source_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 13: "If you had an employer-provided dependent care plan, your employer may have permitted you to carry forward any unused amount from 2024 ... Enter on line 13 the amount you carried forward and used in 2025 during the grace period." Line 12: "Enter the total amount of dependent care benefits you received in 2025 ... Form(s) W-2"
findings.why: Lines 12 through 15 combine both spouses' benefits on a joint return, so line 13 needs both spouses' grace-period carryforwards. The singular 'your employer's' wording leads a joint filer to leave out the spouse's carryforward. The help text does not say to include the spouse's plan.

findings.situation: A filer paid for the care of their spouse, who could not care for themselves and lived with them for more than half of 2025; a spouse is a qualifying person who is never the filer's dependent, but the question's two alternatives leave the spouse out, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.source_text: i2441 p. 1: "2. Your disabled spouse who wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves and lived with you for more than half the year."
findings.why: The gate asks about care for a qualifying person who is not the filer's dependent. The question covers only the 'would be your dependent except' disabled person and the custodial-parent child, so care for a disabled spouse gets no yes.

findings.situation: On a joint return where only the spouse's employer plan provides the benefits and that plan caps the exclusion at $4,000, the filer may enter $5,000, reading 'your dependent care plan' as their own plan only.
findings.source_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "Enter on line 21 the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan ... if your dependent care plan only allows a maximum of $4,000 to be excluded, substitute $4,000"
findings.why: Line 21 must reflect the lower maximum of any plan behind the benefits on line 12, including a spouse's plan. The question says 'your dependent care plan (or plans...)' and tells filers to enter $5,000 'if you do not know of a lower plan maximum', which a filer with no plan of their own could reasonably take as $5,000. The help text does not mention a spouse's plan.

findings.situation: A filer whose spouse died in 2025, who then remarried before year end and files jointly with the new, living spouse, would truthfully answer yes, so the gate opens even though the joint return is not filed as a surviving spouse of the person who died.
findings.source_text: p503 p. 11: "If your spouse died during the year and you file a joint return as a surviving spouse, you may, but aren't required to, take into account the earned income of your spouse who died during the year"
findings.why: The question "Did your spouse die in 2025?" does not tie the death to the spouse on the joint return, and the gate only checks MFJ status. A remarried filer could therefore leave out the living joint spouse's earned income, which the earned income limit requires them to use.
